FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A80
Report road rage that is happening right now by calling 911 at once. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A80
When you call 911 about an aggressive driving act, give where the vehicles were last seen, the plate if known, direction of travel, the road, vehicle colors, any weapons, what happened and whether you were a victim or witness. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A80
Cutting road rage and aggressive driving is central to the mission of the Washington State Patrol, and reports from residents help improve safety. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A81
An informed decision weighs every factor before you act, and such decisions raise your awareness, encourage responsible driving and lower the risk of crashes. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A81
Your decisions are shaped by your knowledge of traffic laws, your experience with safe practices, and the capabilities that come with your age and brain development. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A81
In teen drivers the brain area that handles judgment and decisions is still maturing, so teens may take more risks or misjudge situations and must put safety ahead of speed and peer pressure. [A81]
Why it matters: the guide singles out teens for safety over social pressure, not only for skill.
Source: [A81 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A81
Physical and mental abilities shift with age and older drivers can be hurt more seriously in crashes, yet many stay safe and capable drivers late in life. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A82
The guide's decision approach has three steps: inform yourself with mirror checks and signal your plan to others, prepare the vehicle so you reach the hazard at the right position and speed, and make a final check before the maneuver. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A82
In every change you make on the road, aim to be aware, predictable and smooth. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A82
Solving a problem on the road usually means changing your speed, shifting your lane position, or changing your path to reach a safe place to reassess, while telling others your plan so you do not surprise them. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A83
The OODA loop is Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, and it is called a loop because each situation leads straight into the next one. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A83
In the OODA loop, Observe spots what changed, Orient uses your knowledge to judge what the change means for safety, Decide picks the safest action, and Act carries it out smoothly with clear signals. [A83]
Why it matters: Orient is the understanding step, which learners often merge into Observe.
Source: [A83 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A84
Distractions fall into four groups: inside the vehicle such as phones, food, the radio and passengers; outside such as billboards and crashes; physical such as fatigue or discomfort; and mental such as daydreaming, worry or strong emotion. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A85
Distracted drivers tend to drift from their lane, drive too fast or too slow, miss signals, stop signs and vulnerable road users, and follow too closely. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A85
To avoid distraction, plan ahead, put the phone away and stay observant, which lets you react faster, decide better and feel less stress and fatigue. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A85
Washington defines distracted driving as any activity that pulls attention away from the main job of driving. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A85
No driver of any age or experience may hold an electronic device such as a phone, tablet or gaming device while driving, though hands-free use is permitted. [A85]
Why it matters: holding the device is the offense; hands-free is allowed but can still pull your eyes and mind off the road.
Source: [A85 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A86
An officer can ticket you for breaking the distracted driving law, the fines can be heavy, and fines for violations after your first can be doubled. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A86
Smart drivers are aware inside and outside the car, in control of gas, brake, steering and position, predictable through signals and smooth moves, thoughtful in decisions and intentional in learning. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A86
The guide names four kinds of attention: switching from one focus to another, divided across several tasks, focused on one task, and sustained over a long time. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A87
Help your attention by removing in-car distractions, being well rested, silencing and stowing electronics, limiting passengers and pets, and refusing to multitask. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A87
Searching means actively checking around you with your eyes, while scanning adds turning your head, neck and body to see as much as possible. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A88
Drive at a speed that still lets you search and scan well, because constant searching underpins safe driving. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A88
Scanning ahead means watching for things to steer around, blockages that could hide people, feet, wheels or shadows near parked cars, and what is happening beyond the car in front, so you avoid sudden braking or swerving. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A88
Scanning to the side means watching left and right at intersections, watching for crossing walkers and cyclists, watching for movement behind foliage, and doing a mirror and over-shoulder check before turning. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A88
Look for vehicles and cyclists behind you before a lane change, before turning across a bike lane, and when slowing, backing, or heading down a long or steep hill. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A89
Look behind more often in heavy traffic so that a tailgater or fast-approaching vehicle gives you time to react by changing lanes, tapping the brakes, or adjusting speed. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A89
Respectful driving means everyone buckled up, being fit to drive, showing empathy, respecting others' space, avoiding conflict no matter who is at fault, and caring for the road environment. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A89
Traffic advisories are alerts about current or coming conditions, incidents or closures from transportation officials, traffic centers or navigation apps, delivered by electronic road signs, radio, websites, social media and apps. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A90
Road litter can cause crashes and burning litter can start wildfires, so Washington's littering fines are severe and you and your passengers must secure loads and dispose of trash properly. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A90
State law sets minimum fines for littering and illegal dumping, and local ordinances may differ, so ask local police, the sheriff or a city or county clerk which rules apply. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A90
Leaving a parked car running, especially inside a garage, can release deadly carbon monoxide, so shut the engine off when parked a while, drive smoothly, keep tires inflated and carpool when you can. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A91
Washington's Clean Car Law says a vehicle built in 2009 or later must pass strict clean air standards before anyone can register, license or sell it. [A91]
Source: [A91 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A91
After or during a drive, evaluate yourself by asking whether anything surprised you, whether you surprised anyone, whether your driving was legal, proficient and smooth, and what to change next time, because skills fade without review. [A91]
Source: [A91 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0091]

Glossary: informed decision — acting after weighing all the factors [A81]. OODA loop — Observe, Orient, Decide, Act [A83]. Distracted driving — anything that takes attention from driving [A85]. Scanning — searching with head, neck and body movement as well as eyes [A87]. Traffic advisory — an alert about conditions, incidents or closures [A89].
Memory aid: OODA reads as look, think, choose, do [A83].
